hook.line: Tomás says *cuando llego* and *cuando llegue* a dozen times a day, and they are not the same sentence. One is about every day, the other about one day that hasn't come yet.
hook.es: Cuando llego, Vale ya está aquí.
hook.en: Whenever I arrive, Vale is already here.

examples.es: Cuando llego, Vale ya está aquí.
examples.en: Whenever I arrive, Vale is already here.
When I get there, we'll talk.
Whenever I close up, I clean the tables.
When I close up tonight, I'll clean the tables.
When the lawyer arrived, we started.
What do you do when you get to the café? (to a friend)
What are you going to do when you get there? (to a friend)

rule:
One question decides it: is *cuando* about something that always happens or already happened, or about something still to come?

A habit or a fact: the normal verb. *Cuando llego, Vale ya está aquí.* *Cuando llegó la abogada, empezamos.*

Something still to come: the other vowel. *Cuando llegue, hablamos.*

English doesn't help, because both can be *when I arrive*. Try adding *every time*: if it fits, use the normal verb. Try adding *one day* or *tomorrow*: if that fits, use the other vowel. The rest of the sentence often gives it away too. A future, a command or *voy a* points to the other vowel.
smallPrint: Teachers call this indicative versus subjunctive in time clauses. Only the verb after *cuando* changes: the rest of the sentence stays put.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *tengo* or *tenga* and type the whole sentence: Cuando ___ tiempo, ayudo a Hernando. (This is about a day still to come: When I have time, I'll help Hernando.)
yourTurn.answer: Cuando tenga tiempo, ayudo a Hernando.
yourTurn.why: It is still to come, so it takes the other vowel: *tenga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *salgo* or *salga* and type the whole sentence: Cuando ___ de la reunión, te llamo. (Every time I come out of a meeting, I call you.)
yourTurn.answer: Cuando salgo de la reunión, te llamo.
yourTurn.why: Every time means a habit, and a habit takes the normal verb: *salgo*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Whenever Vale cooks, the café smells great.
yourTurn.answer: Cuando Vale cocina, el café huele rico.
accept: El café huele rico cuando Vale cocina.
yourTurn.why: A repeated thing takes the normal verb: *cocina*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: When Vale cooks (later), the café will smell great.
yourTurn.answer: Cuando Vale cocine, el café va a oler rico.
accept: El café va a oler rico cuando Vale cocine.
yourTurn.why: A single time still to come takes the other vowel: *cocine*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend, about a day still to come: What are you going to do when you finish?
Ask a friend, about a habit: What do you do when you get to the café?
yourTurn.why: A habit takes the normal verb: *llegas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change it from a habit to tonight only: *Cuando cierro, limpio las mesas.*
yourTurn.why: Only the verb after *cuando* changes: *cierro* becomes *cierre*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: When I finished, I called Vale.
yourTurn.why: It already happened, so *cuando* takes the ordinary past, not the other vowel.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Mañana* is still to come, so you need *llegue*.

pitfalls.wrong: Cuando llegue ayer, Vale ya estaba aquí.
pitfalls.right: Cuando llegué ayer, Vale ya estaba aquí.
pitfalls.why: Yesterday already happened, so use the ordinary past. The accent makes *llegué* (I arrived) different from *llegue*.

pitfalls.wrong: Cuando cierre, limpio las mesas todos los días.
pitfalls.right: Cuando cierro, limpio las mesas todos los días.
pitfalls.why: *Todos los días* means a habit, and a habit takes the normal verb: *cierro*.

personal: Say one thing you do every time something happens, and one thing you will do when something happens soon.
